Teacher's note - Vinita, Class 10 class teacher, Monday
At 11 last night Lokesh posted in the class group: "I CAN'T DO THIS ANYMORE!!!! 😤😤" A few students replied with laughing faces. Others replied "same bro."
I couldn't tell whether this was play, frustration or something more serious. Capitals and exclamation marks can mean any of these.
So this morning, before first period, I asked him quietly to walk with me to the staff room. "I saw your post last night. How are you really?"
He laughed, then stopped. "It's the science project. My partner hasn't done anything, and it's due Friday. I was so angry I couldn't sleep."
I asked whether he was feeling unsafe or just very stressed. He said, clearly, "Just stressed, Ma'am. I promise."
I've spoken to his partner, and we've set a check-in for Wednesday. I also told Lokesh my door is open anytime.

Ankita, you asked on this podcast about being fourteen. Okay, I'm Gautam, and fourteen was a rollercoaster.
One evening I remember clearly. At six I was laughing so hard at a video my little sister sent that I fell off the bed. By six-thirty I was snapping at my mother because she asked if I'd done my homework. By seven I was crying in the bathroom, and I honestly couldn't tell you why.
My mother didn't shout back or say, "What's wrong with you?" She just stayed the same. Calm. Dinner at eight. Lights off by eleven, phones out of rooms. She'd knock and say, "Want to talk, or want tea?"
It drove me mad then. Now I think it saved me. I was sleeping about five hours before that. With proper sleep, the swings got smaller.
And when I did want to talk, she was right there, same as always.

qa.q: What time did Gautam's mother set for lights off?
qa.a: Lights off by eleven, phones out of rooms.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling that evening at fourteen?
qa.a: Gautam swung from amused to irritable to tearful within an hour, confused about why the moods changed so fast.

qa.q: What helped Gautam's mood swings settle?
qa.a: The mother's calm, consistent routine, proper sleep, and her gentle, repeated offers to talk or have tea.

qa.q: How might Gautam's mother have felt during those evenings?
qa.a: She was probably worried and sometimes hurt by Gautam's snapping, but chose to stay steady rather than react.

grounding: The spoken account shows a teenager's quickly changing moods, and patient consistency, sleep and gentle talk supporting balance.

At dinner he was cracking jokes and doing impressions of his science teacher. Twenty minutes later, when Papa asked him to clear the plates, he slammed a glass down and shouted, "Why is it always me?" Then, by nine, I found him sitting on the terrace steps, eyes red, not saying anything.

I'm Hansa, and I watched my brother Madhav come home the day the district team list came out. His name wasn't on it. He'd been practising every morning for a year.
Mummy asked, "How did it go?" He shrugged. "Fine. Didn't get in. Whatever." Then he went to his room.
He wasn't slamming doors. He wasn't crying. He ate dinner. He watched TV. If you didn't know him, you'd think he didn't care.
I couldn't tell if he really didn't care or was hiding it. Madhav always plays things down. He hates drama.
Mummy didn't push. But before bed she knocked and said, "I know you said fine. If it stops being fine, I'm here. Tonight or next week."
Three days later, I heard them talking late in the kitchen. He was saying, "I really thought I'd make it."
The door she left open, he walked through when he was ready.

qa.a: Madhav was probably disappointed and hurt after a year of practice, but played it down to avoid drama.

Shalini, you always say "it's nothing" when something's heavy. Let your Yamini Nani tell you about when she did the same.
When I was fifteen, my father fell ill and was in hospital for two months. At school, when friends asked, I shrugged. "It's nothing. He's fine." I didn't want pity. I didn't want to cry in class. So I made it small.
But at home I wasn't sleeping. I'd stopped eating lunch.
My aunt, Kamla Masi, noticed. She never forced me to talk. But every evening she'd sit on the verandah with her knitting and say, "I'm here, if it stops being nothing."
For three weeks I walked past her. Then one night I sat down, and I cried until the knitting was wet.
That open door, Shalini, was the most important thing anyone did for me that year. So when you're ready, I'm here.

qa.a: For two months.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling behind her "It's nothing"?
qa.a: She was frightened and deeply worried about her father, but hid it to avoid pity and crying in class.

qa.a: Kamla Masi leaving the door open every evening without forcing her, until Yamini finally sat down and cried.

Annual Day note - Zainab (Class 9 teacher), Saturday
During the group dance, Urmila slipped on the edge of the stage and landed on one knee in front of about four hundred parents. There was a gasp. Then Urmila threw her head back and laughed, really loudly, got up, and finished the dance with a big grin.
Afterwards several parents and students praised her: "So confident!" "She didn't care at all!"
I wasn't sure. Her laugh had been a bit too loud, and she'd glanced at her friends in the wings before laughing.
In the green room, I asked her quietly, "That was brave. How are you feeling about the slip?"
Her smile dropped. "Ma'am, I wanted to disappear. I laughed so nobody would laugh at me first."
I told her that was a smart, quick move, and that she was allowed to feel embarrassed too. She laughed again, smaller and real.

qa.q: How many parents were watching when Urmila slipped?
qa.a: About four hundred parents.

qa.q: What feelings were behind Urmila's loud laugh?
qa.a: Urmila felt embarrassed and afraid of being laughed at, so she laughed first to cover it.

qa.q: What did Zainab do that helped?
qa.a: She asked quietly and privately how Urmila felt, and accepted both the quick cover and the embarrassment underneath.

qa.q: How did the parents who praised her read the laugh?
qa.a: They read it as confidence and not caring, missing the embarrassment behind it.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a teenager laughing loudly after a slip to cover embarrassment, which others read as confidence.

Counsellor's note - Binita, Class 10, Thursday
Rehana came to see me at lunch, sent by her class teacher. In PE, while the class changed shoes, a group of girls had joked about her old sports shoes: "Did you get them from your grandmother?" Rehana laughed loudly and made a joke back. The teacher, who knows her well, thought the laugh sounded forced.
With me, Rehana smiled for the first ten minutes. "It's fine. It was funny."
I didn't argue. I said, "Sometimes people laugh because it's easier than showing it hurt. If that's what happened, that's okay."
Her smile stayed, but her eyes filled up. "My father lost his job. We can't buy new ones this year. I didn't want them to know."
I told her it was not her fault, and that I'd make sure the PE teacher addressed the teasing without mentioning her family. She left looking lighter.

qa.q: What did the girls joke about?
qa.a: About her old sports shoes.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling behind her smile?
qa.a: Rehana felt hurt and ashamed about the family's money troubles, and laughed to avoid looking weak.

qa.a: She didn't argue or assume, gently allowed for hurt behind a laugh, and offered practical support without exposing Rehana's family.

Sachin had been in Munich for three months on his engineering exchange. The group project was due in two days, and his lab partner Thomas had barely reacted all week.
When Sachin showed him the finished model, Thomas looked at it for ten seconds, nodded once and said, "Good." No smile. No "wow." Then he went back to his laptop.
Sachin's stomach sank. Back home, his friends would have shouted and clapped. Was Thomas annoyed? Did he think it was bad?
With the deadline so close, he couldn't afford guessing. After the lab emptied, he asked, "Thomas, honestly, are you happy with the model? You didn't say much."
Thomas looked surprised. "I'm very happy. It's excellent. In my family, 'good' is a big compliment. We don't jump around." He paused. "You've been worried?"
"A bit."
Thomas smiled, a small one. "I'll try to say 'excellent' more."

Something strange happened at the phone shop today. The clerk mixed up my SIM card, and I had to wait an hour. When she explained the mistake, she was smiling. Smiling! And giggling a little.

Rashmi said not every person does it, but it's common enough that I shouldn't assume.
